lessons.title: comí, viví — two conjugations become one
lessons.gloss: the regular -er/-ir preterite — where two conjugations collapse into one

segments.text: You have the -ar past (hablé). Now the other two. And here Spanish does you a favour it never does in the present tense: -er and -ir verbs take the exact same preterite endings. Learn one set, get both.
Drop -er or -ir, add: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron.

utterances: yo. comer ("to eat"): comí. vivir ("to live"): viví.
tú. comer ("to eat"): comiste. vivir ("to live"): viviste.
él/ella/usted. comer ("to eat"): comió. vivir ("to live"): vivió.
nosotros. comer ("to eat"): comimos. vivir ("to live"): vivimos.
ellos/ustedes. comer ("to eat"): comieron. vivir ("to live"): vivieron.

segments.text: Look down the two columns: the endings are identical. That is not true in the present, where -er and -ir pull apart (comemos vs vivimos). In the past, the two conjugations merge.
The accent works exactly as in Chapter 14: it marks the stressed final vowel — comí, comió. Stress at the end = the past.
These endings are worn-down Latin perfect forms — -ī, -istī, -it. The middle one barely changed at all: Latin -istī becomes Spanish -iste (comiste, viviste). Two thousand years, one dropped vowel.

For -ir verbs, nosotros is the same in present and preterite — vivimos means both "we live" and "we lived" (just like hablamos from Chapter 14). But for -er verbs it differs: comemos (we eat) vs comimos (we ate).

segments.text: Give the five -er/-ir preterite endings. (-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron.) What's the favour Spanish does here? (-er and -ir share one set — though their presents differ.) Which Latin ending is still almost intact? (-istī becomes -iste.) Which nosotros form is ambiguous, and which isn't? (Vivimos is; comemos/comimos are distinct.) Next: the strong preterites, where the accent disappears entirely.

lessons.title: Practice — three families, one question
lessons.gloss: the whole preterite — -ar, -er/-ir, and strong, told apart by where the stress lands

You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The whole map until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You now have the entire everyday past tense. Three families — and one question sorts them: where does the stress land?

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 6 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, yo, tú, él/ella, nosotros, ellos. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Rows 2 and 3 are the same: -er and -ir merged. Rows 1–3 carry accents only on yo and él, where the ending is stressed.
Read any preterite and ask: is the loud syllable the last one?
Yes becomes regular. Accent on yo and él/ella (hablé, hablÓ, comí, comió).
No, it's the stem becomes strong. No accent (TUve, HIce, ESTUvo).
Use context for forms shared by two tenses:

utterances: form: hablamos. could be: we speak / we spoke. which?: either — context decides.
form: vivimos. could be: we live / we lived. which?: either — context decides.
form: comemos / comimos. could be: we eat / we ate. which?: distinct — the vowel tells you.
form: fui. could be: I was / I went. which?: either — ser and ir share it.

segments.text: Which two rows are identical? (-er and -ir.) Which forms take a written accent? (Yo and él/ella of the regular verbs only.) What single test separates regular from strong? (Where the stress lands — ending vs stem.) Which form means both "I was" and "I went"? (Fui.) Which nosotros forms are tense-ambiguous? (Hablamos, vivimos — but not comimos.) Next chapter: talking about the past that kept going — the imperfect.

lessons.title: tuve, hice, estuve — the strong preterites
lessons.gloss: the strong preterites — where the stress moves off the ending and the accent disappears

needs: your eyes for 2 tables that cannot be read aloud
waitUntilStopped: Three of them, all verbs you know
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for 2 tables that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Three of them, all verbs you know and The accent rule, inverted until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Everything so far pushed the stress to the end: hablÉ, comÍ, comIÓ. Now meet the verbs that do the opposite. They pull the stress back into the stem — and so they lose their accent marks entirely. Spanish calls them pretéritos fuertes, "strong" preterites: strong because the stem carries the weight.

blocks.title: Three of them, all verbs you know

segments.text: The stem changes, then one shared set of endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, tener becomes tuv-, hacer becomes hic-, estar becomes estuv-. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Compare the yo and él forms across the three families:

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 5 columns and 3 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: family, yo, él/ella, stressed syllable, accent?. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Say them out loud back to back: hablÓ … TUvo. The written accent isn't decoration — it's telling you where the stress went. No accent on a strong preterite because the stress never left the stem.
Note the yo ending too: -e, not -é (tuve, not tuvé).
Hacer gives hizo, not hico — Spanish swaps c becomes z before o to keep the sound the same. The letter changes so the pronunciation won't.

Because they're old. Latin had two ways to build a perfect, and these verbs kept the "strong" one, inherited whole rather than rebuilt: tenuī becomes tuve, fēcī becomes hice, stetī/stāre becomes estuve. The regular -ar/-er/-ir patterns are the tidy replacements that spread later; the strong verbs are the most-used ones, worn smooth by frequency and never re-made. Notice tuv- and estuv- even share the same -uv- shape.

segments.instruction: "Ayer estuve en casa" ("Yesterday I was at home")
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Ayer estuve en casa" ("Yesterday I was at home")]

segments.text: Why "strong"? (The stem carries the stress.) So why no accent marks? (Because the stress never reaches the ending — the accent only ever marked that.) What's the yo ending? (-e, not -é.) Why hizo and not hico? (c becomes z before o, to protect the sound.) Where do they come from? (Latin's strong perfects — tenuī, fēcī — inherited, not rebuilt.) Next: all three families side by side.
